title: Short Stuff: Ig-pay Atin-lay (Sorry)
summary: Short Stuff episode on pig Latin (also written Ig-pay Atin-lay). Josh and Chuck explain the basic rule (move the initial consonant to the end and add "ay", so "cat" becomes "at-kay"), and how multisyllable words like "curtain" are handled. They trace predecessors dog Latin and hog Latin, including Shakespeare's mock-Latin passage in Love's Labour's Lost, and note Edgar Allan Poe's mention of dog Latin and pig Greek. They date pig Latin to the late 1800s, with an Atlantic description of children's jargon, and offer a theory on why parents tolerated it. They cover the early twentieth-century popularity, including the song "Pig Latin Love" by Arthur Fields (clip planned, public-domain status uncertain) and a Three Stooges short where Curly is taught pig Latin. They classify pig Latin as back slang or a coded language rather than an invented language like Esperanto or Klingon, and survey similar games: France's verlan, Spanish "gaba topo" style doubling, and Japan's bobbigo, with "subushi" for sushi.

segments.title: Opening banter and how pig Latin works
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about how hard pig Latin is to speak fluently and explain the basic rule: move the first letter to the end and add 'ay', so 'cat' becomes 'at-kay'. They discuss multisyllable words like 'curtain' and how fluent speakers scramble each syllable.

segments.title: Dog Latin, hog Latin and Shakespeare
segments.summary: The hosts describe dog Latin and hog Latin as earlier fake-Latin styles, with hog Latin possibly leading to the name pig Latin. They discuss Shakespeare's mock-Latin passage in Love's Labour's Lost, which they say works more like Cockney rhyming slang, and Edgar Allan Poe's mention of dog Latin and pig Greek.

segments.title: Origins of pig Latin as children's slang
segments.summary: Pig Latin was in use by the late 1800s. An Atlantic description calls it a jargon invented by children. Josh offers a personal theory that parents let it continue because they understood it and found it charming.

segments.title: Pig Latin's golden age and the Pig Latin Love song
segments.summary: The hosts describe pig Latin's heyday in the first decades of the twentieth century and the Arthur Fields record 'Pig Latin Love'. They discuss whether a clip can be played because of public-domain uncertainty, then play a short clip.

segments.title: Three Stooges pig Latin lesson
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh mention a Three Stooges short, Tassels in the Air, in which Moe and Larry try to teach Curly pig Latin, and Curly fails and gets slapped. They also mention upcoming Three Stooges episodes.

segments.title: Pig Latin as back slang and coded language
segments.summary: The hosts classify pig Latin as back slang or a coded language, not an invented language like Esperanto or Klingon, because it depends on English vocabulary and grammar and is used to disguise speech.

segments.title: Similar language games in other countries
segments.summary: They survey similar games: France's verlan, a Spanish doubled-vowel-and-P game (gato becomes gaba topo), and Japan's bobbigo, which inserts 'bi' syllables (sushi becomes subushibi).

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up the episode and the show credits are read.
